section.name: Partharo
section.description: Description of Shri Hari's manifestation, childhood sports, divine powers, symbols on His form, and natural behaviors, serving as a preface in 5 parts.

partharos.title: The Manner of Shrihari's Manifestation
partharos.verses:
पातुं धर्ममधर्ममुत्खनयितुं श्रीभक्तिधर्माङ्गतो
जातायोत्तरकोसलेषु दयया सर्वेश्वरेशाय च।
तृप्तिं वाक्यसुधारसैर्विदधते नैजैर्निजानां मुहुस्
तस्मै श्रीहरये नमोऽस्तु सहजानन्दाय सद्वर्णिने॥ १॥
ज्ञानेन धर्मेण युतां विरक्त्या माहात्म्यबोधेन च यो निजस्य।
प्रवर्तयामास भुवि स्वभक्तिं स श्रीहरिर्नोऽस्तु मतिप्रदाता॥ २॥
अज्ञानसंज्ञं गहनान्धकारं निजाश्रितस्वान्तगुहागतं यः।
अपाहरज्ज्ञानदिवाकरः श्रीधर्माङ्गजन्मा जयति प्रभुः सः॥ ३॥
प्रोक्तानियानीहवचोऽमृतानि श्रीस्वामिनातेननिजाश्रितेभ्यः।
तेषां लिखामः कतिचित्तदीयतुष्ट्यै यथाबुद्धि यथाश्रुतं च॥ ४॥
तत्रादौ श्रीहरेस्तस्य जन्मादि-चरितं शुभम्।
कथयामः समासेन तदीयानन्ददायकम्॥ ५॥
partharos.text:
In the center of Golok is the Akshardham of Bhagwan. What is it like? It is as luminous as tens of millions of suns, moons, and fires; it is divine, extremely white, and of the nature of Sat-Chit-Ananda. It is also called Brahmapur, Amritdham, Param Pad, Anant Apar, Brahma, and Chidakash. In that Akshardham, Shri Krishna Bhagwan is ever-residing. What is He like? He is called Purushottam, Vasudev, Narayan, Paramatma, Brahma, Parabrahma, Ishwar, Parameshwar, and Vishnu. And what else is that Bhagwan like? He is beyond Kshar and Akshar, omniscient, the doer of all, the controller of all, the inner-controller (Antaryami) of all, the cause of all causes, Nirguna, self-luminous, and independent. He is worthy of being worshipped by infinite tens of millions of Muktas who are Brahma-rupa. The creation, sustenance, and dissolution of infinite tens of millions of universes (brahmands) are His divine play (leela). He is the instigator (prerak) of Prakriti-Purush, Kaal, Pradhan-Purush, Mahat-tattva, and others, which are His powers (shaktis). He is the King of kings of infinite tens of millions of universes. He is eternally in a youthful form (kishor-murti), as beautiful as tens of millions of Kamadevas (kandarpa), and His complexion is dark-hued like a fresh rain-cloud. He is adorned with various types of priceless and divine garments and ornaments. He wears alligator-shaped earrings (makara-shaped kundals) in His ears and a crown studded with various types of jewels on His head. His lotus-eyes are sharp like the petals of an autumn lotus. His limbs are smeared with beautiful, fragrant sandalwood paste. He plays the flute (venu) with a sweet melody. He is worshipped by Radhikaji and Lakshmiji. He is served by His personified weapons like Sudarshan and others, and by countless attendants (parshads) like Nand, Sunand, and Shridama. His form is endowed with light like tens of millions of suns and moons. He is possessed of infinite tens of millions of auspicious, redemptive qualities. His lotus-feet are served by the powers of Dharma, Gyan, Vairagya, and other divine virtues, as well as the eight yogic powers (siddhis) like Anima. He is praised by the four Vedas in personified form. He is the supporter and source of the Chaturvyuha like Vasudev, the twenty-four forms like Keshav, and all the incarnations (avatars) like Varaha.
Such Shri Krishna Purushottam Bhagwan, endowed with all His divine powers and majesties (aishwarya), manifested in the land of Koshal. He did so to establish Ekantik Dharma on the earth, to protect and grant bliss to His Ekantik devotees like Dharma, Bhakti, and the sages like Marichi, to bring redemption (kalyan) to countless souls, and to eradicate unrighteousness (adharma).
Now, the manner in which Bhagwan manifested is described in brief: At one time, the sages like Marichi came to Badrikashram to have the darshan of Shri Nara-Narayan Bhagwan. Hearing of this, Dharmadev, along with his wife Murti, also came to have the darshan of Shri Nara-Narayan. Then, after having the darshan of the sage Shri Nara-Narayan, who was seated along with Uddhav in the assembly of those sages, and being welcomed and honored by Shri Nara-Narayan, Dharmadev sat in that assembly. The sages like Marichi had previously related the accounts of the events in Bharat-khand (the Indian subcontinent) before the sage Shri Narayan. Dharmadev, along with those sages and Uddhav, listened to these accounts from the lotus-mouth of the sage Shri Narayan with single-minded focus. At that time, from Mount Kailas, the sage Durvasa came to have the darshan of the sage Shri Narayan. Since no one welcomed or honored him, the sage Durvasa cursed all of them, including Dharmadev, saying: 'All of you who have insulted me shall take birth as human beings in Bharat-khand, and there you shall suffer insults and hardships at the hands of demons (asuras).' Hearing such a curse, Dharmadev pacified the sage Durvasa with words full of great humility. Durvasa then said: 'You were all deeply absorbed in listening to the discourse of the sage Shri Narayan, which is why you did not see me and I was not welcomed. I did not know this, and that is why I cursed you. However, my curse cannot be averted. Nevertheless, along with this curse, I grant you a boon: O Dharmadev! You and your wife Murti will take birth in a Brahmin family as humans, and there this Narayan Rishi will be born as your son. He will liberate you and these sages from my curse and protect you all from the miseries inflicted by the demons.' Saying this, the sage Durvasa returned to Mount Kailas. Thereafter, the sage Shri Narayan spoke to all of them, including Dharmadev: 'If I wish to avert this curse that has befallen you without any fault, I am capable of doing so, and it will be averted. However, at present, having gained strength from the influence of Kali-yug in Bharat-khand, unrighteousness and demons have increased greatly. By My own wish, this curse has occurred, and I have accepted it. Therefore, O Dharma! I will become your son, destroy the demons and unrighteousness, protect all of you, and establish Ekantik Dharma on the earth. Therefore, do not worry at all and assume human bodies on the earth.' Hearing these words and bowing to the sage Shri Narayan, all of them, including Dharmadev, departed for the earth to assume human bodies.
Now we describe the manner in which Dharma and Murti manifested: In the land of Koshal, there is a town named Ittar, in which lived a Sarvariya Brahmin of the Samaveda named Balsharma Pande. From him, through his wife named Bhagyavati, Dharmadev manifested in Samvat 1796, on the day of Kartik Sud 11 (Ekadashi), after midday. His father performed his birth-rites and other sacraments according to scriptural injunctions and named him Devsharma on the twelfth day. In that same land of Koshal, in a village named Chhapaiya, through a Brahmin named Krishna Sharma Trivedi and his wife named Bhavani, Murti manifested in Samvat 1798, on the day of Kartik Sud 15 (Purnima), in the evening. Thereafter, she grew day by day and began to perform intense devotion to Shri Krishna Bhagwan, which is why she came to be known by the name Bhakti.
Thereafter, Bhakti's father, Krishna Sharma, performed the marriage of his daughter Bhakti with Devsharma (the incarnation of Dharma) according to scriptural rites, and kept his son-in-law in his own village at his home. Then, Devsharma, along with his wife Bhakti, took support of the duties of the householder stage (grihasthashram) and performed devotion to Shri Krishna Bhagwan. Seeing him behave with extreme steadiness in righteousness (dharma), all the people began to address him by the name 'Dharma'.
Thereafter, Dharma and Bhakti suffered intense harassment from the demons. To alleviate their suffering, Dharma and Bhakti went to Vrindavan along with the sages like Marichi and worshipped Shri Krishna Bhagwan. Consequently, Bhagwan became pleased with them and, showing them His form as He eternally resides in His Akshardham, He spoke to Dharma and Bhakti: 'O Dharma! O Bhakti! The demons who are causing you distress were previously killed by Me during My incarnation as Krishna. They harbor enmity towards Me; therefore, knowing you to be Mine, they torment you. To destroy those demons, I will manifest from you as the son of Narayan Rishi and become famous by the name Harikrishna. I will protect you and the sages from the miseries of the demons and liberate you from the curse of Durvasa. I will also eradicate the demons and unrighteousness, and establish Ekantik Dharma on the earth.' Saying this, Shri Krishna Bhagwan disappeared and resided within the lotus-heart of Dharma. Thereafter, Dharma and Bhakti, filled with supreme joy, returned from there to their village and performed devotion to Shri Krishna Bhagwan. Because Bhagwan was thus pleased with Dharma, all the people began to address him by the name Hariprasad.
And then, after several months had passed, from Hariprasadji, through Bhakti, Shri Krishna Bhagwan manifested in Samvat 1837, on the day of Chaitra Sud 9 (Navami), when ten ghadis of the night had passed. At that time, a grand celebration took place in the home of Hariprasad, and Indra and other devas, chanting 'victory, victory' and sounding kettle-drums, showered flowers. The celestial nymphs (apsaras) danced, the gandharvas sang, and the sages gave blessings. The minds of the devas and sadhus became extremely pleased, while the minds of the demons were instantly struck with terror. The women residing in that village sang auspicious songs and blessed Hari in His infant form. At that time, gentle, fragrant, and cool breezes blew. The sky, along with the hosts of stars, became extremely clear. After that, Hariprasadji had the birth-rites of his son performed by Brahmins according to scriptural rites and gave various types of charity to the Brahmins.

partharos.title: Shrihari's Childhood Sports and Forest Travels
partharos.text:
Thereafter, on the sixth day after His birth, when baby-snatching spirits (bal-grahas) like Kotara came to kill Bhagwan in His infant form, Bhagwan burned and drove them away by His mere glance. When Bhagwan reached the age of three months and eleven days, the sage Markandeya came to the house of Hariprasadji in the guise of a Brahmin. At that time, Hariprasadji welcomed and honored the sage with great respect, and knowing him to be an astrologer, said, 'Please perform the naming ceremony of our son.' The sage, pleased, proceeded with the naming ceremony and said, 'O Hariprasadji! This son of yours will remove all your adversities, and will also remove all the adversities of those who take refuge in Him. Since His birth is under the zodiac sign of Cancer, His name will be Hari. Furthermore, because the body of this son of yours is dark-complexioned (krishna-varna) and He will attract the minds of His refugees to His form, and because He is born in the month of Chaitra, He will be famous by the name Krishna. Even though these two names are distinct, they will combine to form a third name, Harikrishna. And this son of yours, by virtue of the five qualities of detachment (tyag), wisdom (gyan), austerity (tap), righteousness (dharma), and yoga, will be like Shiva; therefore, He will be renowned among the people by the name Neelkanth. In addition, because this son of yours has the sign of a lotus on His hand and the signs of a vajra, an upward line (urdhva-rekha), and a lotus on His feet, He will be the ruler of hundreds of thousands of people. This son of yours will be endowed with infinite redemptive virtues and will protect you from all hardships.' Having said this, the sage Markandeya stopped, and Hariprasadji offered him a large amount of monetary donations (dakshina) and valuable new clothes and ornaments. The sage stayed there for one day and then departed to perform a pilgrimage to Prayag. After that, Hariprasadji and Bhaktimata were overjoyed to hear of their son's qualities. Thereafter, Shrihari, through His childhood sports (leelas), brought great joy to His parents and relatives, and grew day by day like the waxing crescent moon. Then, in the fifth month, Hariprasadji sat his son on the earth for the first time. In the sixth month, he taught Him to eat solid food for the first time (annaprashan). In the seventh month, he had His ears pierced. When the third year began, he performed the tonsure ceremony (chaul-sanskar, i.e., shaving the birth-hair). On that very day, a demon named Kalidatt, who possessed magical powers, came to kill Bhagwan. Bhagwan confused and deluded him by His mere glance, and the demon died by repeatedly dashing against trees.
Thereafter, due to the harassment of the demons, Hariprasadji abandoned Chhapaiya village and, along with his family, resided in Ayodhyapuri. In the fifth year, Hariprasadji taught his son the alphabet (reading and writing) for the first time. In the eighth year, gathering grand materials, he performed the sacred thread ceremony (yagnopavit) for his son. Receiving the sacred thread from his father, Shrihari adhered to the vows of a lifelong celibate (naishtik brahmachari) and studied the Vedas. Under his father's guidance, He studied and listened to the Vedas, Shastras, Puranas, histories (Itihasas), and scriptures of righteousness (Dharmashastras), and came to know their true essence. From all these scriptures, He extracted four essential summaries. From the Shrimad Bhagavatam Purana, He extracted the 'Fifth Canto' and 'Tenth Canto'. From the Skanda Purana, He extracted the 'Vasudev Mahatmya'. From the Mahabharata (history), He extracted the 'Bhagavad Gita', 'Vidur Niti', and 'Vishnu Sahasranam'. From all the Dharmashastras, He extracted the 'Yajnavalkya Smriti'. Thus, having extracted these four summaries, He had them written into a small manuscript (gutko), which He kept with Him daily. When Shrihari reached eleven years of age from His birth, He initiated His mother Bhakti into devotion (bhakti) accompanied by dharma, gyan, and vairagya, thereby granting her divine liberation and freeing her from the curse of Durvasa. A few months later, Shrihari gave His father Hariprasadji the true knowledge of His own form, granting him divine liberation and freeing him from the curse of Durvasa.
Thus, having attained divine liberation, Dharma and Bhakti remained constantly near Shrihari in their divine bodies. Thereafter, without asking His relatives, under the pretext of taking a daily bath, and driven by the force of intense detachment (tivra vairagya), Shrihari abandoned His home and set out alone towards the north to perform austerities. What was He like? He wore a loincloth (kaupin) along with a lower garment, a deer skin, and held a staff of palash wood, a white sacred thread (yagnopavit), a double-stranded tulsi rosary around His neck, and the mark of the Urdhvapundra tilak with a red chando. He had matted locks (jata) on His head and a waist-string of munja grass. In His hands, He carried a rosary (jap-mala), a water-pot (kamandalu), an alms-bowl, and a water-filter. He wore around His neck a small pouch containing a Shaligram and Balmukund. On His shoulder, He carried the manuscript containing the four summaries. Clad in this guise, Shri Neelkanth Brahmachari swam across the Sarayu river and went towards the north. Walking for several days, He reached a vast forest in the foothills of the Himalayas. Walking further, He reached the Himalayan mountains. After walking in the mountains for several days, He came to Muktinath and performed severe austerities, pleasing Suryanarayan. Staying there for several months, He then walked towards the south and wandered for twelve months in a dense forest in the foothills of the Himalayas. Thereafter, in that forest, Shri Neelkanth Brahmachari saw Gopal Yogi sitting under a banyan tree practicing yoga. He stayed with the yogi for a year, learning the eightfold yoga (Ashtanga Yoga), and giving the yogi the knowledge of His own form, He granted him the state of perfection (siddha-gati). Then, walking northward, Shri Neelkanth Brahmachari reached the pilgrimage site named Adivarah. Proceeding from there, He reached a town named Sirpur in Bengal. The king of that town, named Siddhavallabh, was highly righteous, and at his request, Shri Neelkanth Brahmachari stayed there for the four months of the monsoon (chaurmasa). In that city, He subdued the pride of the demons who were worshippers of Kali and Bhairav and were arrogant about their yogic powers, and by His own power, He protected His servant, a sadhu named Gopaldas, from the black magic of the demons. Also in that city, there was a Brahmin from the Tailang country who was learned in the Vedas, Shastras, and Puranas. He had accepted a large charity of elephants and other gifts from the king. Because of this, although the Brahmin was fair-complexioned, he turned dark-complexioned. That Brahmin then came to take refuge in Shri Neelkanth Brahmachari to expiate his sin. By His power, He freed him from that sin, whereupon his black color disappeared and he became fair-complexioned as before. Proceeding from there, Shrihari reached a village near the temple of Kamakshi Devi. In that village, there was a Brahmin worshipper of Mahakali who was so arrogant that whenever any sadhu or Brahmin pilgrim came to his village, he would defeat them using black magic and make them his disciples. That Brahmin came and directed all his occult powers, mantras, and black magic against Shrihari. However, Shrihari was not affected in the least, and by His own power, He humbled the pride of that Brahmin and made him His disciple. Walking from there, Shrihari reached the Navlakha mountain, where there are nine hundred thousand abodes of Siddhas, and in nine hundred thousand places, flames of fire emerge along with water reservoirs. Showing His form to the Siddhas residing on that mountain, He descended and reached the pilgrimage site named Balwa Kund. Proceeding from there, Shrihari reached the confluence of Ganga Sagar, bathed there, and then crossed the bay in a boat to reach Kapilashram, where He stayed for a month having daily darshan of Kapilji. From there, He went to Jagannathpuri. Residing there for several months, He incited mutual enmity and caused battles among many demons who were a burden to the earth, thus destroying them. Thereafter, Shri Neelkanth Brahmachari walked towards the south and reached the pilgrimage site named Adikurma. Then, walking through a vast forest, He reached Manaspur. The king of that city, named Satradharma, took refuge in Him, and through that king, He subdued the demons. Proceeding from there, Shri Neelkanth Brahmachari reached Venkatadri. From there, He went to Shiv-Kanchi and Vishnu-Kanchi. From there, He went to Shri Rangam and stayed for two months, and through discourses with Vaishnavas, He removed the corrupt practices (durachar) among them by His divine influence. Proceeding from there, Shrihari reached Setubandh, bathed in the ocean, and stayed there for two months, having daily darshan of Rameshwar Mahadev. Walking from there, He had darshan of Vishnu named Sundarraj, and walking from there, He travelled for five days in a dense forest without finding any food or water. On the sixth day, at midday, He found a well in the forest. Drawing water with His kamandalu, He bathed, and then sat under a banyan tree performing His daily rituals and worshipped the Shaligram. He placed the Shaligram in a vessel and began to bathe it with water poured from His kamandalu. However, whatever water He poured, the Shaligram drank it up. In this manner, it drank up five to seven kamandalus of water. Realizing that it was satisfied after drinking water, He worshipped the Shaligram with sandalwood paste and other items and began to think, 'Since the Shaligram was so thirsty, it must also be hungry. But I have no food offerings (naivedya) to present. What shall I feed Vishnu?' While He was thinking this, Shiva and Parvati, riding on Nandi in the guise of travellers (kapadi), arrived and stood there. Seeing Shri Neelkanth Brahmachari worshipping the Shaligram in this manner, they offered Him sattu (flour of roasted grains) and salt. He mixed the sattu in water, offered it to Vishnu, and then ate it himself. Proceeding from there, Shri Neelkanth Brahmachari reached Bhutpuri, where He had darshan of and worshipped the image of Ramanujacharya, and from there He came to Kanyakumari (Kumarika Kshetra). From there He went to Padmanabh. From there He went to Janardan. From there, after having darshan of Vishnu named Adikeshav, He reached the mountain range named Malayachal. He stayed there for five days, having darshan of Vishnu named Sakshi-Gopal. Proceeding from there, Shri Neelkanth Brahmachari went to Pandharpur and stayed for two months having darshan of Vishnu named Vitthalnath. Embracing Vitthalnath, He departed from there and reached Dandakaranya. After circumambulating Dandakaranya, He came to Nasik. Having darshan of Tryambakeshwar Mahadev, He came to the Tapi river. Proceeding from there, He crossed the Narmada river and reached the Mahi river. Crossing the Mahi and Sabarmati rivers and crossing the Bhal region, He came to Bhimnath. From there, Shri Neelkanth Brahmachari had darshan of Shiva named Gopnath, and performing the pilgrimage of Panch-Tirthi, He came to the port of Mangrol. Thus performing pilgrimages, Shri Harikrishna Bhagwan, wherever He went, eradicated unrighteousness and established Ekantik Dharma. He granted His darshan to the people residing in those pilgrimage places, accepted their food and water, and liberated them from the cycle of worldly existence (sansar).

partharos.title: Shrihari's Divine Play, Work, and Majesties
partharos.text:
Thereafter, departing from there, Shri Neelkanth Brahmachari arrived in Lojpur on Samvat 1856, Shravan Vad 6. And in Lojpur, He saw Muktanand Swami and other sadhus, who were the disciples of Shri Ramanand Swami, the incarnation of Uddhav. Recognizing them to be devotees of Shri Krishna Bhagwan endowed with saintly qualities, He stayed with them. Having stayed there for several months, He departed from there along with those sadhus and reached the village of Piplana, located in the shadow of Mount Girnar. On Samvat 1856, Jyeshtha Vad 12, He had the darshan of Shri Ramanand Swami, who was residing at the home of a Brahmin named Narsinh Mehta. What was Ramanand Swami like? His form was fair and robust, he wore white garments, and he was in the guise of a lifelong celibate (naishtik brahmachari). Bowing down to him with prostrations (dandvat pranam) and embracing him, Shri Neelkanth Brahmachari sat near him. Seeing Shri Neelkanth Brahmachari, Swami was filled with great joy and asked about His entire background. Then, Shri Neelkanth Brahmachari described His birthplace, family, parents, lineage (gotra), Veda, pravar, guru, and chosen deity (Ishtadev) exactly as they were. He also described in detail and in sequence His detachment (vairagya), how He abandoned His relatives, how He resided in the forest, how He performed various types of austerities, how He mastered the eightfold yoga (Ashtanga Yoga), how He performed pilgrimages, and how He defeated the hypocritical gurus residing in those pilgrimage places. Hearing this account, Swami became extremely pleased and spoke to Shri Neelkanth Brahmachari: 'O Brahmachari! You belong to us; because your father Dharma first received Bhagavati initiation (diksha) from us at Prayag-kshetra, and by our command, he stayed in the land of Koshal, imparting the teachings of devotion to Shri Krishna Bhagwan along with righteousness (dharma) to seekers of liberation. You are the son of that Dharma, and in qualities, you are even greater than your father.' Hearing these words of Swami, Shri Neelkanth Brahmachari was extremely pleased and remained near him. Thereafter, on Samvat 1857, Kartik Sud 11, He received the Bhagavati initiation from Swami. At that time, Swami named Him 'Sahajanand' and also gave Him a second name, 'Narayan Muni'. He then served Swami with great love and devotion. Seeing Narayan Muni to be endowed with all saintly qualities and extremely capable, and handing over the leadership of the fellowship (dharma-dhur) to Narayan Muni, Ramanand Swami left his body on Samvat 1858, Margashirsha Sud 13, and returned to Badrikashram, thereby being liberated from the curse of Durvasa.
Thereafter, Shri Sahajanand Swami performed the post-death rituals of His guru according to scriptural rites and took up the leadership of the fellowship. He comforted the sadhus, brahmacharis, and householders who had taken refuge in Ramanand Swami by instructing them in holy scriptures. Showing them His extraordinary divine powers (alaukik pratap), He attracted their minds to Himself. After that, Swami Shri Sahajanandji Maharaj, surrounded by His disciples who were renunciant sadhus, brahmacharis, and householder devotees (satsangis), wandered through all the regions such as Sorath, Halar, Kutch, Jhalavad, Kathiawad, Bhal, and Gujarat, spreading His divine influence, promoting devotion (bhakti) accompanied by dharma, gyan, and vairagya, eradicating unrighteousness, and subduing the hypocritical demonic gurus.
And wherever Shriji Maharaj travelled, the people of those regions, seeing the extraordinary divine powers (alaukik aishwarya) of Shriji Maharaj, took refuge in Him in large numbers and performed devotion to the manifest form of Shriji Maharaj. Thereafter, for their joy and to strengthen their faith, Shriji Maharaj showed His various divine powers by putting them into trance (samadhi). In this trance, to some people, He showed Himself in the form of Shri Krishna in the center of Golok, which is Akshardham, accompanied by Lakshmi, Radhika, and attendants like Shridama. To some, He showed Himself in the form of Vishnu in Vaikunth-lok, accompanied by Lakshmi and attendants like Nand and Sunand. To some, He showed Himself in the form of Mahapurush in Shvetadvip, accompanied by the Niranna Muktas. To some, He showed Himself in the form of Bhumapurush in the Avyakrit abode, accompanied by His powers like Lakshmi and His attendants. To some, He showed Himself in the form of Nara-Narayan in Badrikashram, accompanied by the sages. To some, He showed Himself in the form of Yogeshwar in the Ocean of Milk (Kshirsagar), accompanied by Lakshmi and Sheshnag. To some, He showed Himself in the form of Hiranyapurush in the solar orb (surya-mandal). To some, He showed Himself in the form of Yagnapurush in the sacrificial fire (agni-mandal). To some, He instantly made them hear the sound of Pranava. To some, He showed His light, which was as luminous as tens of millions of suns. To some, He showed Himself as Brahma, who is beyond the states of waking (jagrat), dreaming (svapna), and deep sleep (sushupti), characterized as Sat-Chit-Ananda, and known as the witness (Drashta). To some, He showed Himself in the form of Viratpurush, the support of the universe, who is described in the Purusha Sukta. To some, He showed the abodes and glories of the devas residing in the earth and sky. To some, He showed individually the devas like Ganesh who reside in the six chakras (Adhara and others). Sometimes, He would give direct and visible darshan to His devotees residing a hundred leagues away. Sometimes, to the astonishment of His devotees, He would eat the food offerings (naivedya) placed before His image in the homes of His devotees residing far away. Sometimes, when His devotees were about to leave their bodies, He would go there to take them to His abode, and would also give direct and visible darshan to other devotees or non-devotees residing in that village. Seeing Shri Sahajanandji Maharaj exhibiting such extraordinary divine powers to both seekers of liberation and others, thousands of people were filled with great wonder. They abandoned their respective beliefs and gurus, took exclusive refuge in Shriji Maharaj, and performed devotion to His manifest form. Thereafter, many disputants came to debate with Shriji Maharaj, but no one was capable of defeating Shriji Maharaj in debate. Seeing the extraordinary divine powers and influence of Shriji Maharaj, all those disputants bowed down to Him and said, 'O Maharaj! You are Parameshwar; therefore, please graciously grant us the darshan of our respective chosen deities (Ishtadevs).' Hearing their prayers, He made them sit down and, by His divine influence, instantly put them into trance (samadhi). Then, all of them, whose vital breath and pulses were suspended by the mere sight of Shriji Maharaj, saw Shriji Maharaj within their hearts in the form of their respective chosen deities. Among them, those Vaishnavas who were followers of the Vallabh clan, the Nimbarka sect, or the Madhvi sect, saw Him in the form of Shri Krishna, the captivator of hearts, surrounded by the group of gopis in Vrindavan and performing His childhood sports. Those of the Ramanuja sect saw Him in the form of Lakshmi-Narayan, accompanied by attendants like Nand, Sunand, Vishwaksen, and Garuda. Those who were Ramanandis saw Him in the form of Shri Ramachandraji, accompanied by Sita, Lakshman, and Hanuman, seated on a divine throne. Those who followed the school of Shankaracharya saw Him in the form of the light of Brahma (Brahma-jyoti). Those who were Shaivas saw Him in the form of Shiva, accompanied by Parvati and the Pramatha attendants. Those who were worshippers of Surya saw Him in the form of Hiranyapurush residing in the solar orb. Worshippers of Ganapati saw Him in the form of Maha-Ganapati. Worshippers of Devi saw Him in the form of Devi. Jains saw Him in the form of Tirthankars. Muslims saw Him in the form of the Prophet (Pegambar). Thus, seeing Shriji Maharaj in the form of their respective chosen deities through trance, and realizing Him to be the cause of all causes, they abandoned their respective sects, took firm refuge in Shriji Maharaj, and performed devotion to His manifest form. In this way, by His divine influence, Shri Sahajanandji Maharaj destroyed the primal ignorance (ajnana) of the souls, and properly established Ekantik Dharma on the earth, which had been lost.
Moreover, He had many almshouses (sada-vrat) established through His wealthy householder devotees. He also had non-violent sacrifices (yagnas) like Vishnu-yaga, Maha-rudra, and Ati-rudra performed. In those yagnas, He satisfied thousands of Brahmins with sweet foods and had various kinds of charity distributed to them. He repeatedly satisfied sadhus, Brahmins, and deities through worship and feasts. He repeatedly eradicated unrighteousness and hypocrisy. And wherever Shriji Maharaj travelled, He explained in detail and accurately to His devotees the divisions of the duties of class and life-stage (varnashram dharma), self-realization (atma-gyan), detachment (vairagya), the knowledge of His own form, and devotion (bhakti) accompanied by the knowledge of His greatness (mahatmya). In this way, bringing daily joy to His devotees, Shriji Maharaj, bound by the devotion of His devotee, King Abhay, his sisters, and his son, resided at their home in the town of Gadhada. Residing there, on the occasion of festivals such as Janmashtami, Ram Navami, Prabodhini Ekadashi, Hutashani, and Annakut, He would summon grand materials and organize large festivals. During those festivals, Paramahansas, brahmacharis, and householder devotees from various regions came repeatedly to have the darshan of Shriji Maharaj. They worshipped Shriji Maharaj with various garments, ornaments, sandalwood paste, flowers, and other worship materials. During those festivals, Shriji Maharaj had various types of food items prepared and repeatedly satisfied thousands of sadhus and Brahmins in many ways.

partharos.title: Description of the Marks on Shrihari's Form
partharos.text: First, we write the marks on the form (murti) of such Shri Sahajanand Swami Maharaj: In the soles of both lotus-feet of Shriji Maharaj, there is an upward line (urdhva-rekha). What is it like? It starts near the toes and extends to both sides of the heels. Near the base of the big toe of the right foot, there is a mark of a barley grain (yava) meeting the upward line. On the sole of the right foot, on both sides of the upward line, there are the marks of a lotus, an elephant goad (ankush), a flag, an octagon, a thunderbolt (vajra), a swastika, and a rose-apple fruit (jambu-phal). On the nail of the right big toe, there is the mark of a vertical red line. On the outer side of that same big toe, there is a mole (til). On the side of the toe next to the big toe, on the side facing the big toe, there is a mole. On the outer side of the smallest toe of the right foot, near the nail, there is a mole. On the left side of the upward line on the left foot, there are two black marks close to each other. Meeting that same upward line, near the base of the toes, there is the mark of space (vyom). On the sole of the left foot, on both sides of the upward line, there are the marks of a bow, a water-pot (kalash), a fish, a triangle, a cow's hoof-print (go-pad), and a half-moon (ardha-chandra). The soles of both feet are reddish. The nails of the big toes and other toes of both feet are reddish, elevated, and lustrous. On the big toes and other toes of both feet, there are marks of fine, soft hair (rom). On both big toes and the two toes next to them, there are marks of friction from wearing wooden sandals (chakhadis). On the outer ankles of both feet and below them, there are marks of friction from sitting in yogic postures (asanas). Five fingers (tasus) above the right ankle, on the shin, there is a small mole. On the outer side of the thigh of that same leg, there is a large mark. Five fingers above the left ankle, on the shin, there is a large mole, and right next to it, slightly above, is a small mole. On the outer side of the knee of that same leg, there is a mark. On both sides of the waist, there are dark marks from the friction of wearing a dhoti. On His abdomen, which is ever cool, there are three folds (trivali). On both sides of His deep and round navel, there are moles; of these, the one on the right is on the rim of the navel, and the one on the left is slightly away from the navel. On the right flank, there is a large mole, and next to it is another small mole. Two fingers above the navel, there are three moles, of which one is on each of the two abdominal muscles and one is in the middle; and two fingers above that middle mole, there is another mole. On the left side, above the flank and below the armpit, there is a vertical row of four large moles, and next to it, on the outer side, there is another vertical row of four small moles. On His chest, there is the Shri-vatsa mark of fine hair. In the center of the chest, there is a large, slightly reddish mark in the shape of a half-moon, five fingers wide, which is slightly more elevated on the right side. In the middle of this mark, slightly to the left, there is a large mole; two fingers to the left of that mole, there is another mole; and two fingers to the left of that, above the left breast, there is a mole. Above both breasts, there are two marks of seals (chhap). Near the inner side of the right arm, there are four moles in a vertical row. On the right arm, three fingers below the shoulder, there is the mark of a seal; and next to that seal mark, on the outer side, there are four small moles. Below the right elbow and above the wrist, there are two moles. Half a finger above the base of the pinky finger of the right hand, there is a small mole. Three fingers below the shoulder of the left arm, there is the mark of a seal. Two fingers below the left elbow, on the upper part of the arm, there is a mole. Between the index finger and middle finger of the left hand, there is a mole. Near the nail of the index finger of the left hand, on the inner side, there is a small mole. On the wrist of the left hand, there is a mole. The nails of both hands are reddish, elevated, and lustrous, and the tips of those nails are very sharp. The palms of both hands are reddish, and the lines on the palms appear slightly dark. Eight fingers above the base of both palms, there are two marks of seals. Both elbows are dark. In the middle of the collarbone hollow, there is a mole, and slightly away from that mole, there is a small mole. Below the chin, there is a mole. Two fingers below the left shoulder, on the back, there is a large mole with hair, and below that mole, there is another mole, and below that, yet another mole. Two fingers below the neck, on the left side of the spine, there is a mole. On the right shoulder blade, there is a small mole. In the middle of the back, to the right of the spine, there are four moles. Near the right side of the nose, there is a large mole, and slightly above that mole, below the corner of the eye, there is a small mole. Fine wrinkles form above and below the lower and upper eyelashes of both eyes. On the nose, there are small, fine marks of smallpox scars. In the mouth, on the lower right side, on the first molar tooth, there is a dark mark. His tongue is reddish like a lotus petal. Inside the left ear, there is the mark of a dark spot. On His broad and elevated forehead, there are two vertical lines in the shape of a tilak. On the right side of the forehead, below the hairline, there is a mark. On the lobe of the right ear, there is a small mole. On the crown of the head, there is a large mole. Near the front of the tuft of hair (shikha), there is a mole, and to the right behind the shikha, there are three moles. Apart from these, there are several other small moles on the body. The form (murti) of Shriji Maharaj is endowed with supreme beauty, elegance, and sweetness. His form is robust and extremely resplendent. His form is such that it captivates the minds and eyes of the devotees who have His darshan. His form is dark-hued (Ghanshyam) and endowed with a peaceful nature. The height of Shriji Maharaj's form is exactly the same as the height of the murti of Shri Gopinathji in Durgapattan (Gadhada). All the limbs, hands, feet, etc., of Shriji Maharaj's form are exactly as described in the science of physiognomy (Samudrik Shastra). Thus, the marks on the form of Shriji Maharaj have been written according to memory.

partharos.title: Shrihari's Natural Behaviors
partharos.text:
Now, we write the natural behaviors (chesta) of Shriji Maharaj: It is Shriji Maharaj's daily habit to wake up when four ghadis or three ghadis of the night remain, and brush His teeth. Thereafter, having bathed and dried His body with a washed, dry, fine cloth, He stands up and squeezes the garment He has worn by bringing it between His two thighs and wringing it out with both hands. He then wipes His thighs and legs, and properly pulls and wears a washed, thick, white fine cloth. Having a preference for wearing white garments, Shriji Maharaj then wraps another washed, fine, white cloth around His body, steps onto His wooden sandals (chakhadis), performs His daily morning rituals, and goes to have His meal. He sits on His seat in a clean and pure dining area. When sitting to eat, He places the cloth wrapped around His upper body behind His ears, keeping His ears uncovered. While eating, He faces east or north, sits with His left leg folded and His right leg upright, resting the elbow of His right hand on it. While eating, He has a habit of repeatedly drinking water. During the meal, if He finds any food item particularly delicious, He has it served to a favorite devotee of His choice. While eating, He has a habit of belching and rubbing His hand over His stomach. Sometimes, when He is pleased with a devotee, He gives or sends them His plate of sanctified food (prasadi). When He wishes to serve the sadhus, He places the shoulder-cloth (khes) on His left shoulder, ties the ends of the khes tightly around His waist, and serves. While serving, He repeatedly mentions the names of the items like laddoos and jalebis, walking up and down the rows. He has immense faith, respect, and joy in feeding and serving the sadhus and devotees. Sometimes, during the monsoon and autumn seasons, knowing the water of the Ghela river near Durgapattan to be clean, He goes to bathe along with the sadhus and devotees. Praising the water of the river and bringing joy to His devotees, He plays in the water with them in various ways. When diving into the water, He blocks His ears, eyes, and nose with the thumbs and fingers of both hands. After diving, when He emerges after a long time, He rubs His right hand over His face and rinses His mouth. Sometimes, standing in the middle of the river current, He has the sadhus clap and sing devotional songs (kirtans), and He also claps along with them and sings kirtans with great enthusiasm. When He enters the water to bathe or when He emerges after bathing, He holds the hand of a strong devotee who is dear to Him. Emerging from the river water along with His devotees whose faces are filled with joy at His sight, He stands on the river bank and, as before, wrings out the garment He has worn, wipes His body, and tightly wears a dry, white khes. He then ties a white turban (fento) on His head. While tying the fento, He leaves a decorative tuft (chhoglu) at the end, and He pulls one wrap of the fento over His eyebrow. Thereafter, placing a white khes on His left shoulder and tying the ends of the khes tightly around His waist, He mounts a beautiful, strong mare or horse. Surrounded on all sides by thousands of His devotees, and bringing joy to the eyes of the devotees who are having His darshan, He returns to His lodging. When Shriji Maharaj walks, He drapes a white shawl (pachedu) or white khes crosswise over His left shoulder and walks while swinging His right hand. Sometimes, He walks while swinging His right hand, which holds a handkerchief. Sometimes, He places His left hand on His waist and walks while swinging the handkerchief in His right hand. Shriji Maharaj has a natural habit of walking fast. When He walks, the devotees walking behind Him have to run to keep pace with Him. When He walks wearing wooden sandals, the sandals make a clicking sound. Sometimes, when He is standing or walking slowly, ready to perform some work, He has a habit of clenching His right fist and gently tapping His right thigh. Sometimes, when there is a large crowd of people and dust rises, He places His handkerchief over His nose and face. Sometimes, He sits on a cot (dholiyo), sometimes He sits on a mattress covered with a clean sheet, sometimes He sits on a cushioned seat (gadi), and sometimes He sits on a small square mat (chaklo). Sometimes, He sits cross-legged. Sometimes, He sits with His knees bound by a cloth. Whenever He sits, He mostly leans against a bolster. Sometimes, while sitting on a cot or a seat, He leans against a bolster, stretches His legs, and places one leg over the other. Sometimes, while sitting, He vertically traces the upward line on His left sole with the finger of His right hand. Sometimes, He has a natural habit of pressing His tongue under the teeth on one side while sitting. Sometimes, while sitting, He twists His neck to both sides to crack it. Sometimes, He has His back massaged by His devotees; when He does so, He places a bolster under His chest. Wherever Shriji Maharaj sits casually, He turns a tulsi rosary (mala). Sometimes, playfully, He doubles the rosary and turns two beads at a time. Sometimes, while conversing, He folds the rosary, places it between the palms of both hands, and rubs it. Sometimes, when He does not have a rosary, He counts the joints of His fingers. Sometimes, He sits meditating with His lotus-eyes closed. Sometimes, He sits meditating with His lotus-eyes open. Sometimes, He starts and wakes up from meditation. Sometimes, when the sadhus play musical instruments and sing kirtans before Him, He sits meditating. Sometimes, snapping His fingers, He begins to sing along with those sadhus. Sometimes, when the sadhus clap and sing kirtans, He claps along with them and sings. Sometimes, when the sadhus play musical instruments and sing kirtans before Him, or when a scriptural discourse (katha) is being read before Him, or when He is speaking to His devotees, He moves closer to them. While having a discourse read, He repeatedly utters the word 'Hare'. Even while performing other activities, sometimes He suddenly utters the word 'Hare' out of habit; when He realizes this, He looks at the devotees sitting near Him and smiles gently. Sometimes, when He is joyfully conversing, or having a discourse read, or having kirtans sung, or sitting in deep thought, if someone comes in between to ask about meals, or to perform worship, or to offer a garland, He becomes very annoyed. Sometimes, sitting in the assembly of His devotees, He discourses on devotion accompanied by dharma, gyan, and vairagya. Sometimes, He discourses on the core essence of scriptures such as Yoga, Sankhya, Pancharatra, and Vedanta. Sometimes, sitting in the assembly of His devotees, when He discourses on dharma and other topics, He first raises both His arms, claps His hands to quieten everyone, and then speaks. Sometimes, when there is a large assembly of a great multitude of devotees and He wishes to discourse on dharma and other topics, He stands up and claps to quieten everyone so that He can be heard even from afar. Sometimes, while discoursing, He becomes so single-mindedly absorbed that He does not even realize when His upper cloth slips off. Sometimes, sitting in the assembly of His devotees, He has the sadhus and householder devotees sitting near His face ask and answer questions among themselves. If someone asks a difficult question and no one knows the answer, He answers it, bringing joy to everyone. Sometimes, while conversing, He crushes a bouquet of flowers or a large flower with both hands. Sometimes, while conversing, He has a natural habit of twisting the ends of His handkerchief. Sometimes, during festivals, He accepts the grand worship offered with love by His devotees who have come from various regions. Sometimes, during festivals, when many devotees come together to worship Him, He accepts the flower garlands offered by them with both His hands, with His lotus-feet, or with His staff. Sometimes, by His mere glance, He puts His devotees into trance (samadhi), and sometimes He instantly wakes them from trance. Sometimes, when He is sitting in the assembly and wishes to call a devotee near Him, He calls the devotee by gesturing with His lotus-eyes or with the finger next to His thumb (index finger). Sometimes, knowing jasmine garlands or lemons and other fruits to be cool, He repeatedly presses them against His eyes. Sometimes, He has scriptural discourses read and listens to them, or He Himself delivers discourses, or He speaks about Bhagwan, or He has kirtans sung and sings along with them, or He has temples built, or He feeds sadhus and Brahmins—He has a habit of never remaining idle without performing such virtuous activities. Whatever work He begins related to bhakti and dharma, He has a great urgency to complete it. When He needs to sneeze, He first looks for His handkerchief, places it before His face, and sneezes loudly so that it can be heard from afar; whenever He sneezes, He sneezes two or three times in succession. When He yawns, He rubs His eyes two or three times with His hand while uttering the words 'Hari, Hari, Hari'. He has a preference for the service performed by single-minded, desireless devotees. When He laughs heartily at something humorous, He holds His handkerchief before His face and laughs. Sometimes, seeing sadhus or dear devotees who have come to Him from other regions, He is pleased, instantly stands up, embraces them, and asks them for news of those regions. Sometimes, during festivals, He affectionately embraces the sadhus who have remained near Him and are now departing to other regions by His command. Sometimes, pleased with a devotee, He places both His hands on their head. Sometimes, pleased, He places His lotus-feet on the chest of a devotee. Sometimes, when He sees a devotee who has eagerly obeyed His command immediately, or a devotee who has returned after properly fulfilling His command, He is pleased and places His lotus-feet on their chest. Sometimes, pleased with a devotee, He gives them His sanctified flower garlands, decorative tassels (toras), armlets, or His garments and ornaments. Being extremely generous by nature, even if a highly valuable object is dear to Him, if He resolves in His mind to give it, He immediately gives it to a deserving recipient without any delay. Sometimes, He cracks the joints of His fingers and toes, and sometimes He has the devotees sitting near Him crack His fingers and toes. Sometimes, seeing or hearing of a distressed creature, He instantly expresses compassion by saying 'Ram, Ram, Ram'. Furthermore, sometimes, seeing any human in distress, He feels compassion in His heart and out of pleasure, He helps that person with food, clothing, and other items to alleviate their suffering. Sometimes, seeing someone being beaten, out of compassion and being unable to bear the sight, He instantly shouts out to stop it. Sometimes, if He hears anyone speaking ill of a sadhu or a devotee in His presence, He becomes very annoyed, disregards the speaker, and reprimands them. Sometimes, when He feels some discomfort in His body, He checks the pulse of His right hand with the fingers of His left hand. When He rises from the assembly, He has a habit of saying 'Jai Sachchidanand' or 'Jai Swaminarayan' and bowing to the sadhus before rising. When He travels on horseback, sometimes, playfully, He rests one of His legs over the neck of the horse while riding. When He goes to sleep, while still awake, He first vertically traces His forehead with His fingers as if applying a tilak. When He is about to sleep, He asks for His rosary and sleeps while turning it in His right hand. When He sleeps, He has a habit of sleeping with His face uncovered. If someone touches Him even slightly while He is fast asleep, He instantly starts and wakes up, asking 'Who is it?'
In this way, the natural behaviors of Shriji Maharaj have been written according to memory, and there are several other behaviors as well. Residing in Gadhada, to dispel the doubts of His devotees, Shriji Maharaj delivered discourses on the five topics: swadharma, atma-gyan, vairagya, the knowledge of His own form, and devotion accompanied by the knowledge of His greatness. These discourses, along with those He delivered after travelling to other villages, are recorded as the Vachanamrut. From these, the discourses of several days are written here for the pleasure of His Ekantik devotees, according to memory and intellect.
